{{Short description|Mathematical formula in complex analysis}}
{{distinguish|Jensen's inequality}}

In [[complex analysis]], '''Jensen's formula''' relates the average magnitude of an [[analytic function]] on a circle with the number of its [[root of a function|zeros]] inside the circle. The formula was introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Johan Jensen (mathematician)|first=Johan|last= Jensen|year=1899}} and forms an important statement in the study of [[entire function]]s.

== Formal statement ==

Suppose that <math>f</math> is an analytic function in a region in the [[complex plane]] <math>\mathbb{C}</math> which contains the [[closed disk]] <math>\mathbb{D}_r</math> of radius <math>r>0</math> about the origin, <math>a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n</math> are the zeros of <math>f</math> in the interior of <math>\mathbb{D}_r</math> (repeated according to their respective multiplicity), and that <math>f(0)\neq 0</math>. 

'''Jensen's formula''' states that<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Ahlfors |first=Lars V. |title=Complex analysis : an introduction to the theory of analytic functions of one complex variable |date=1979 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |isbn=0-07-000657-1 |edition=3rd |location=New York |chapter=5.3.1, Jensen's formula |oclc=4036464}}</ref>

:<math>\log |f(0)| = -\sum_{k=1}^n \log \left( \frac{r}{|a_k|}\right) + \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \log|f(re^{i\theta})| \, d\theta.</math>

This formula establishes a connection between the [[Absolute value|moduli]] of the zeros of <math>f</math> in the interior of <math>\mathbb{D}_r</math> and the average of
<math>\log|f(z)|</math> on the boundary circle <math>|z|=r</math>, and can be seen as a generalisation of the mean value property of [[harmonic function]]s. Namely, if <math>f</math> has no zeros in <math>\mathbb{D}_r</math>, then Jensen's formula reduces to
:<math>\log |f(0)| = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \log|f(re^{i\theta})| \, d\theta,</math>
which is the mean-value property of the harmonic function <math>\log |f(z)|</math>.

An equivalent statement of Jensen's formula that is frequently used is
:<math>\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \log |f(re^{i\theta})| \, d\theta - \log |f(0)| = \int_0^r \frac{n(t)}{t} \, dt
</math>
where <math>n(t)</math> denotes the number of zeros of <math>f</math> in the disc of radius <math>t</math> centered at the origin.

{{Math proof|title=Proof<ref name=":0" />|proof=
It suffices to prove the case for <math>r=1</math>. 
# If <math>f</math> contains zeros on the circle boundary, then we can define <math>g(z) = \frac{f(z)}{\prod_k (z-e^{i\theta_k})}</math>, where <math>e^{i\theta_k}</math> are the zeros on the circle boundary. Since <math display="block">\int_0^{2\pi} \ln|e^{i\theta} -e^{i\theta_k}| d\theta = 2\int_0^\pi \ln(2\sin \theta)d\theta= 0,</math> we have reduced to proving the theorem for <math>g</math>, that is, the case with no zeros on the circle boundary.
# Define <math display="block">F(z) := \frac{f(z)}{\prod_{k=1}^n(z-a_k)}</math> and fill in all the removable singularities. We obtain a function <math>F</math> that is analytic in <math>B(0, 1+\epsilon)</math>, and it has no roots in <math>B(0, 1)</math>.  
# Since <math>\log |F| = Re(\log F)</math> is a harmonic function, we can apply [[Poisson integral formula]] to it, and obtain <math display="block">\log |F(0)|=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} \log |F(e^{i \theta})|\, d \theta
	  = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \log|f(e^{i\theta})| \, d\theta -\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \log |e^{i\theta} - a_k| \, d\theta.</math> where <math>\int_0^{2\pi} \log|e^{i\theta} - a_k| \, d\theta</math> can be written as <math display="block">\int_0^{2\pi} \log|e^{i\theta} - a_k| \, d\theta
	  = \int_0^{2\pi} \log|1 - a_ke^{-i\theta}| \, d\theta = Re \int_0^{2\pi} \log(1 - a_ke^{-i\theta}) \, d\theta.</math>
# Now, <math>\int_0^{2\pi} \log(1 - a_ke^{-i\theta}) \, d\theta</math> is a multiple of a contour integral of function <math>\log (1-z)/z</math> along a circle of radius <math>|a_k| < 1</math>. Since <math>\log(1-z)/z</math> has no poles in <math>B(0, |a_k|)</math>, the contour integral is zero.
}}

== Applications ==

Jensen's formula can be used to estimate the number of zeros of an analytic function in a disk. Namely, if <math>f</math> is a function analytic in a disk of radius <math>R</math> centered at <math>z_0</math> and if <math>| f |</math> is bounded by <math>M</math> on the boundary of that disk, then the number of zeros of <math>f</math> in a disk of radius 
<math>r<R</math> centered at the same point <math>z_0</math> does not exceed
:<math> 
\frac{1}{\log (R/r)} \log \frac{M}{|f(z_0)|}.
</math>

Jensen's formula is an important statement in the study of value distribution of entire and meromorphic functions. In particular, it is the starting point of [[Nevanlinna theory]], and it often appears in proofs of [[Hadamard factorization theorem]], which requires an estimate on the number of zeros of an entire function.

Jensen's formula is also used to prove a generalization of [[Paley-Wiener theorem]] for [[quasi-analytic function]]s with <math>r \rightarrow 1</math>.{{sfn | Paley | Wiener | 1934 | pp=14-20}} In the field of [[control theory]] (in particular: [[polynomial_matrix_spectral_factorization|spectral factorization methods]]) this generalization is often referred to as the '''Paley–Wiener condition'''.{{sfn | Sayed | Kailath | 2001 | pp=469–470}}

==Generalizations==
Jensen's formula may be generalized for functions which are merely meromorphic on <math>\mathbb{D}_r</math>. Namely, assume that
:<math>f(z)=z^l \frac{g(z)}{h(z)},</math> 
where <math>g</math> and <math>h</math> are analytic functions in <math>\mathbb{D}_r</math> having zeros at <math>a_1,\ldots,a_n \in \mathbb{D}_r\setminus\{0\}</math>
and 
<math>b_1,\ldots,b_m \in  \mathbb{D}_r\setminus\{0\}</math>
respectively, then Jensen's formula for meromorphic functions states that

:<math>\log \left|\frac{g(0)}{h(0)}\right| = \log \left |r^{m-n-l} \frac{a_1\ldots a_n}{b_1\ldots b_m}\right| + \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \log|f(re^{i\theta})| \, d\theta.</math>

Jensen's formula is a consequence of the more general '''Poisson&ndash;Jensen formula''', which in turn follows from Jensen's formula by applying a [[Möbius transformation]] to <math>z</math>. It was introduced and named by [[Rolf Nevanlinna]]. If <math>f</math> is a function which is analytic in the unit disk, with zeros
<math>a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n</math> located in the interior of the unit disk, then for every <math>z_0=r_0e^{i\varphi_0}</math> in the unit disk the '''Poisson&ndash;Jensen formula''' states that

:<math>\log |f(z_0)| = \sum_{k=1}^n \log \left|\frac{z_0-a_k}{1-\bar {a}_k z_0} \right| + \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} P_{r_0}(\varphi_0-\theta) \log |f(e^{i\theta})| \, d\theta.</math>

Here,
:<math> P_{r}(\omega)= \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} r^{|n|} e^{i n\omega} </math>
is the [[Poisson kernel]] on the unit disk.
If the function <math>f</math> has no zeros in the unit disk, the Poisson-Jensen formula reduces to
:<math>\log |f(z_0)| = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} P_{r_0}(\varphi_0-\theta) \log |f(e^{i\theta})| \, d\theta,</math>
which is the [[Poisson kernel|Poisson formula]] for the harmonic function <math>\log |f(z)|</math>.
